practiceSet.title: U2.LT3 Practice: Isotopes and Isotope Notation
practiceSet.description: Practice defining isotopes, reading and writing hyphen and nuclear notation, counting protons, neutrons, and electrons, and finding the most common isotope.

activity.title: U2.LT3 Relearning: Isotopes and Isotope Notation
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can explain what isotopes are and use isotope notation to describe them.

**Think of two backpacks of the same model.** Same brand, same color, same name tag. One has 2 textbooks inside and the other has 4. One is heavier, but it is still the same backpack with the same name tag. Isotopes work the same way: the **protons** are the name tag (they give the atom its identity), and the **neutrons** are the extra books (they add mass but do not change what the atom is). Isotopes are like identical twins who don't weigh exactly the same.

**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. **What stays the same:** the number of protons, the **atomic number**, and (in a neutral atom) the number of electrons. Because the electrons are the same, isotopes react the same way. **What changes:** the number of neutrons, so the **mass number** (protons + neutrons) changes too.

**Hyphen notation** is element name – mass number, like potassium-40 or C-12. **Nuclear notation** puts the mass number on top and the atomic number on the bottom, to the left of the symbol: $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$. The bottom number can be left off ($^{40}\text{K}$) because the symbol already tells you the atomic number. **Counting:** p⁺ = atomic number; n⁰ = mass number − atomic number; e⁻ = p⁺ if the atom is neutral.

**Average atomic mass** is the decimal number on the periodic table. It is a weighted average of all of the element's isotopes, so it is **closest to the mass number of the most common isotope**. When no mass number is given, round the average atomic mass. Our notes also say an isotope is most stable when the numbers of p⁺ and n⁰ are the same, and an unstable nucleus comes from too many or too few neutrons.

**Worked example 1:** Write potassium-40 in nuclear notation and count its particles (K, atomic number 19). Step 1: The mass number is the number after the dash, 40. Step 2: Put 40 on top and 19 on the bottom: $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$. Step 3: p⁺ = 19. Step 4: n⁰ = 40 − 19 = 21. Step 5: e⁻ = 19 (neutral). Answer: 19 protons, 21 neutrons, 19 electrons.

**Worked example 2:** Are $^{6}_{3}\text{Li}$ and lithium-7 isotopes? Step 1: Both are lithium, atomic number 3, so both have 3 protons. Step 2: Neutrons: 6 − 3 = 3 and 7 − 3 = 4. Step 3: Same protons, different neutrons. Answer: yes, they are isotopes of lithium.

**Worked example 3:** Magnesium (Mg, atomic number 12) has an average atomic mass of 24.305. Find its most common isotope. Step 1: Round 24.305 to 24; that is the mass number. Step 2: Hyphen notation: magnesium-24. Nuclear notation: $^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}$. Step 3: n⁰ = 24 − 12 = 12. Answer: magnesium-24, with 12 neutrons.

**Watch out for:** writing the atomic number on top; using the number of neutrons in the hyphen name instead of the mass number; thinking a new top number makes a new element (only the bottom number, the protons, does that); thinking isotopes have different protons; and mixing up the whole-number mass number with the decimal average atomic mass.
prompts: Explain why carbon-12 and carbon-13 are still the same element. Use the words protons and neutrons.
An isotope of sulfur (S, atomic number 16) has 17 neutrons. Write it in hyphen notation and in nuclear notation, and show how you found the mass number.
Neon's average atomic mass is 20.180. Which isotope of neon is most common? Write it in both notations and give its numbers of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Are argon-40 (atomic number 18) and potassium-40 (atomic number 19) isotopes of each other? Explain using protons and neutrons.
